texts.0: SP, due to lateral stick and throttle inputs that were not coordinated while tracking the Leader in landing configuration, did not hold the fingertip lateral separation about the 10 ft reference point. Spacing opened well beyond the 20 ft allowance and at one point closed inside the reference point, and the IP had to intervene on the controls to restore safe wingtip clearance. The excursion was not recognized by SP before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to a coarse correction technique that chased the Leader's wing instead of stabilizing on the briefed sight picture, worked the approach with lateral spacing at the 20 ft outer limit. Position was brought back toward the reference point only after repeated verbal prompts from the IP, and each correction was delayed. Spacing was not reduced inside the 10 ft reference point.
texts.2: SP, due to a small lag in matching the Leader's roll inputs, allowed lateral spacing to open to roughly 15 ft, between the 10 ft and 20 ft tolerances. The deviation was recognized promptly and closed back onto the fingertip reference with a smooth aileron and power correction, with no prompting and no IP input.
texts.3: SP held fingertip lateral separation within 10 ft of the reference point throughout the approach. Corrections were small, early, and taken off the briefed sight picture rather than by chasing the Leader's wing. Lateral position remained stable through the configuration change and the descent.
texts.4: SP flew lateral separation essentially on the reference point, with deviations barely perceptible from the lead cockpit. The sight picture was held with continuous, near-imperceptible aileron and power inputs from the roll-out to the break-off. Position quality did not degrade at any stage of the approach.
texts.marginal: SP kept lateral separation inside the fingertip standard, but the working position sat consistently toward the outer edge of the band and the corrections were larger than the situation required. The trend was toward opening rather than holding the reference point, particularly in the turns. SP is expected to tighten the sight picture and apply smaller, earlier lateral inputs.

error_modes.label: Vertical position on the Leader's wing line

texts.0: SP, due to an unstable pitch reference and incomplete trim technique in the landing configuration, did not maintain the wing-level relationship with the Leader. Vertical displacement went well above the 10 ft high limit and then below the 5 ft low limit, placing the aircraft under the Leader's wing line, and the IP intervened to reposition the aircraft. The vertical excursion continued to develop before SP recognized it.
texts.1: SP, due to pitch corrections applied late and without a supporting power change, sat at the 10 ft high edge of the permitted band for extended segments of the approach. The wing-level relationship was re-established only after verbal direction from the IP, and each recovery was slow. The low side of the band was not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed pitch response as the Leader adjusted descent rate, allowed vertical position to move into the upper part of the permitted band, approaching but not exceeding the 10 ft high tolerance. SP recognized the drift immediately and re-established the Leader's wing line with a coordinated pitch and power input, unprompted.
texts.3: SP maintained position on the Leader's wing level inside the permitted 10 ft high and 5 ft low band for the whole approach. Pitch and power were coordinated so that descent rate matched the Leader and vertical position stayed stable. No stepping above or below the wing line was observed.
texts.4: SP flew the vertical relationship essentially on the Leader's wing line, with departures from that line negligible. Descent rate matching was continuous, so no corrective pitch step was required at any point. Vertical position quality was unchanged from the roll-out to the break-off.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the vertical band but worked habitually on the high side, using the 10 ft allowance as the normal position rather than the wing line. The tendency became more pronounced as the descent rate changed. SP is expected to fly the Leader's wing line as the target and reserve the tolerance for corrections.

texts.0: SP, due to power lag that was left uncorrected against the Leader's speed changes, did not hold the observance angle that defines the fingertip longitudinal position. The angle went well aft of the 55 deg boundary during the deceleration and then swung forward of the Leader's wing line in the recovery, and the IP took control to re-establish the position. The sweep of the angle was not arrested by SP's own inputs.
texts.1: SP, due to throttle inputs made in large steps rather than anticipated against the Leader, worked the approach at an observance angle of about 50 deg, at the outer allowance. The angle was brought forward only when the IP called it, and the tighter position was not sustained. The 55 deg boundary was not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late power reduction as the Leader stabilized on final, allowed the observance angle to move aft to about 40 deg, between the 35 deg and 45 deg tolerances. The aft drift was identified quickly and corrected back toward the 30 deg reference with a measured power addition, with no prompting required.
texts.3: SP maintained the observance angle within 5 deg of the 30 deg reference throughout the approach. Longitudinal position was held with anticipated throttle inputs matched to the Leader's speed changes rather than reactive corrections. The angle stayed steady through the configuration change and the descent.
texts.4: SP held the observance angle effectively on the 30 deg reference, with variation barely detectable from the lead cockpit. Power was modulated continuously so that no visible fore-and-aft motion developed against the Leader. Longitudinal position quality was maintained to the point of break-off.
texts.marginal: SP kept the observance angle inside the standard but consistently toward the aft edge, and the recoveries to the reference angle were slow. The tendency to sit aft was more pronounced whenever the Leader changed airspeed. SP is expected to anticipate the power requirement so that the reference angle, not the tolerance, becomes the working position.

error_modes.label: Station keeping through Leader's turns up to 30 deg bank
error_modes.source: general:null (fingertip criteria applied); conditions:1/ No1 executes maneuvers up to 30 deg of bank

texts.0: SP, due to a skill-based error in control input as the Leader rolled into the turn, did not maintain the fingertip geometry through the maneuvering. The aircraft went acute and high on the inside of the turn and then fell aft and wide on the roll-out, outside the fingertip tolerances in both axes, and the IP intervened to re-establish the position. No recovery was initiated by SP before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to bank matching applied after the Leader's roll rather than with it, held the position at the outer fingertip tolerances through each turn up to 30 deg of bank. Corrections followed only after the IP called the geometry, and the position was regained slowly on the roll-out. The outer tolerances were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late bank input on entry to the turn, allowed the geometry to move outside the tighter fingertip band while remaining within the outer allowance. SP recognized the developing angle and re-matched bank and power on the roll-out, restoring the sight picture without prompting and without IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained the fingertip position through the Leader's maneuvering up to 30 deg of bank. Bank was matched with the Leader's roll and power was adjusted for the change in required thrust, so the position held on entry, in the turn and on the roll-out.
texts.4: SP flew the turns with the sight picture essentially locked, showing no visible change in geometry between wings level and 30 deg of bank. Roll inputs were matched to the Leader's initiation and the roll-out was anticipated. Position through maneuvering was indistinguishable from position in level flight.
texts.marginal: SP held the fingertip position through the turns, but the geometry loosened on every entry and was recovered only during the roll-out. The pattern repeated rather than improving through the approach. SP is expected to match the Leader's roll rate at initiation so that position does not have to be regained afterwards.

error_modes.label: Landing configuration management while holding position
error_modes.source: execution:landing configuration into the flight area / instrument or straight-in approach; general:null

texts.0: SP, due to configuration changes made without the accompanying power and pitch compensation, did not maintain the wingman position while establishing the landing configuration. Gear and flap selection produced pitch and drag changes that took the aircraft outside the fingertip tolerances, and the IP intervened to re-establish the position before the approach continued. Selections were also made out of step with the Leader.
texts.1: SP, due to a slow response to the trim change with gear and flaps extended, allowed the position to reach the outer fingertip tolerance at each configuration change. Position was regained only after the IP directed the correction, and the same degradation repeated at the next selection. The tolerances were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a small lag in adding power as the landing configuration was completed, drifted outside the tighter tolerance during the configuration change while remaining inside the outer allowance. The deviation was recognized straight away and the position was restored with a coordinated power and pitch input, without prompting.
texts.3: SP established and maintained the landing configuration while holding the wingman position inside the fingertip tolerances. Gear and flap selections were made in step with the Leader and the pitch and drag changes were compensated as they occurred. Position quality was unaffected by the configuration change.
texts.4: SP configured for landing with no detectable movement in the sight picture. Power was led into each selection so that the drag change produced no position excursion, and the selections stayed in step with the Leader without a call. Position remained constant throughout the configuration sequence.
texts.marginal: SP completed the landing configuration within standards, but each selection produced a visible loosening of the position that then had to be corrected. The pattern indicates power is being applied after, rather than with, the configuration change. SP is expected to anticipate the drag and trim change so that the sight picture stays constant.

error_modes.label: Closure and power control on the approach
error_modes.source: general:null (fingertip criteria, longitudinal and lateral separation)

texts.0: SP, due to throttle inputs made in large uncoordinated steps, did not control closure on the Leader during the approach. Overtake developed to a rate that could not be stopped with power alone and separation reduced inside the reference point, so the IP took control and repositioned the aircraft. The closure trend was not identified by SP in time to be corrected.
texts.1: SP, due to throttle corrections that were consistently one step behind the Leader's power changes, produced repeated overtake and fall-back cycles that carried the position to the outer tolerances. Each cycle was arrested only after a verbal call, and the oscillation persisted for the length of the approach. Separation was not reduced inside the reference point.
texts.2: SP, due to late recognition of a small overtake as the Leader stabilized on final, allowed closure to develop beyond the tighter tolerance while remaining inside the outer allowance. SP identified the rate early enough to stop it with a smooth power reduction and re-established the position unassisted.
texts.3: SP controlled closure on the Leader accurately throughout the approach. Power was modulated in small anticipatory inputs so that overtake and fall-back rates were stopped before they became apparent in the sight picture. No large throttle excursions were required.
texts.4: SP flew the approach with closure rates that never became visible in the sight picture. Throttle work was continuous and fine, matched to the Leader's changes as they were initiated rather than after they took effect. No corrective power excursion was needed at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP controlled closure inside the standards, but the corrections were larger than required and produced a low-amplitude oscillation that persisted through the approach. The technique remains reactive rather than anticipatory. SP is expected to use smaller and earlier power inputs to damp the closure rather than reverse it.

error_modes.label: Visual reference priority between Leader and cockpit

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the cockpit instruments during the approach, did not keep the sight picture on the Leader as the primary reference. Position degraded outside the fingertip tolerances in both lateral and vertical axes while attention was inside the cockpit, and the IP intervened before SP recognized the trend. The deviations went undetected as they developed.
texts.1: SP, due to prolonged attention on the instrument panel while in formation, allowed the position to reach the outer tolerances each time the scan went inside. The Leader was reacquired and the position corrected only after verbal prompting, and the pattern repeated at every check. The tolerances were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that dwelt too long on the airspeed indication during the configuration change, allowed the position to move beyond the tighter tolerance while staying inside the outer allowance. SP returned to the Leader as the primary reference promptly and corrected the position without any prompting.
texts.3: SP kept the Leader as the primary visual reference throughout the approach, taking instrument checks in short glances that did not degrade the position. The required cockpit checks were completed with no measurable movement in the sight picture.
texts.4: SP maintained the sight picture continuously, integrating the required cockpit checks into short peripheral glances with no effect on position. Attention priority between the Leader and the cockpit was managed with no visible cost to the formation geometry.
texts.marginal: SP held the position within standards, but glances inside the cockpit were longer than necessary and each return to the Leader required a small correction. The pattern was consistent rather than isolated. SP is expected to shorten instrument checks and use peripheral cues so that the sight picture is not interrupted.

error_modes.label: Approach discipline and coordination with Leader and IP

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of assertiveness in stating that the position could not be regained, continued the formation approach after the wingman position had broken down. The approach was flown to a point where safe separation from the Leader was no longer assured, and the IP directed the break-off and took control. No call to move out or go around was made by SP.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to voice a position that was no longer sustainable, continued the approach at the outer fingertip tolerances instead of moving out and rejoining. Corrective action followed only after the IP stated the requirement, and the intention was never passed to the Leader. Safe separation was preserved throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation in making the call as the position loosened, was late in advising the intention to correct, but recognized without prompting that the position had moved outside the tighter tolerance. SP re-established the fingertip position and passed the required call with no IP input, and the approach continued within the standards.
texts.3: SP flew the formation approach with the required discipline, holding the wingman position stable and stating intentions to the Leader whenever a correction was required. The briefed decision points for continuing or breaking off were applied as briefed.
texts.4: SP managed the approach with clear and timely communication to the Leader and no ambiguity about position or intention. The wingman position was never in doubt and the briefed decision points were applied without hesitation. Coordination remained effective through the whole approach.
texts.marginal: SP met the discipline standard, but calls to the Leader were made later than the developing situation warranted and intentions were stated tentatively. Under increasing workload the tendency was to fly the correction silently. SP is expected to state position and intent early and unambiguously.

error_modes.label: Torque held below the 20 percent minimum on the approach

texts.0: SP, due to pulling torque well below the 20 percent minimum in order to kill an overtake, was left without engine response when power was demanded again. The aircraft fell aft and wide past the outer fingertip allowance, opening beyond 30 ft of lateral separation with the observance angle outside 55 degrees, and the IP added power and recovered the position. The spool up delay caused by the low power setting was not identified by SP.
texts.1: SP, due to repeatedly setting torque under the 20 percent minimum while checking closure, met the same acceleration lag each time power was reapplied. Position swung out to the outer tolerance, about 30 ft of lateral separation with the observance angle at the 45 to 55 degree edge, and was regained only after the IP called for power. The tolerances themselves were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to one power reduction that went just under the 20 percent torque floor while stopping an overtake, absorbed a slow spool up and drifted aft past the tighter band, out to roughly 25 ft of lateral separation while staying inside the outer allowance. SP recognized the sluggish response straight away, restored torque above the minimum and re-established the position without prompting.
texts.3: SP kept torque at or above the 20 percent minimum throughout the approach so that engine response stayed immediate. Closure was controlled with small throttle movements around a serviceable power setting and lateral separation stayed inside 20 ft with the observance angle within 30 plus or minus 5 degrees. No large power excursion was required.
texts.4: SP flew the whole approach with the throttle worked in a narrow band well clear of the 20 percent minimum, so every correction produced immediate thrust. Lateral separation sat on the 10 ft reference point and the observance angle held 30 degrees with no visible movement in the sight picture. Power was never allowed to reach a setting from which recovery would be delayed.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the position within standards, but torque was allowed to touch the 20 percent minimum on two occasions and the resulting acceleration lag turned small fall backs into larger recoveries. The trend is toward using the throttle as a brake rather than as a rate control. SP is expected to keep power above the minimum so that engine response remains available.

error_modes.label: Configuration change made off the single gear and flap signal

texts.0: SP, due to expecting a second signal for the flaps after the gear, left the flaps up when Number 1 directed the landing configuration with the single briefed signal. The drag mismatch produced an unchecked overtake that drove the aircraft forward inside the 45 degree observance limit and closed the lateral separation inside the 10 ft reference point, so the IP intervened to stop the closure and directed the configuration. The missed part of the directive was not detected by SP.
texts.1: SP, due to configuring only after the Leader's gear was seen travelling rather than on Number 1's signal, was consistently late on each selection. The drag and pitch mismatch carried the position out to the outer allowance, about 30 ft of lateral separation with the observance angle at the 55 degree edge, and the selections were completed only after the IP prompted. The tolerances were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed reading of Number 1's visual signal while the scan was fixed on the wing reference, started the configuration change a beat late and allowed the position to open past the tighter band to roughly 25 ft of lateral separation, still inside the outer allowance. SP picked up the drag change quickly, matched the Leader's deceleration and closed the position back down unassisted.
texts.3: SP acted on Number 1's single signal and lowered gear and flaps together with the Leader. The configuration change was flown in step and the position stayed within the tighter fingertip band, lateral separation inside 20 ft and the observance angle within 30 plus or minus 5 degrees. No prompt or repeat of the signal was needed.
texts.4: SP took the configuration directive on the first signal and moved the gear and flap handles with the Leader's, so both aircraft configured as one. The sight picture did not move through the selection, with lateral separation on the 10 ft reference point and no change in the observance angle. The directive was acknowledged without any delay in the visual scan.
texts.marginal: SP configured on Number 1's signal and stayed within standards, but each selection was started a noticeable beat after the signal was given and the position had to be re-closed afterwards. The pattern shows the signal is being confirmed twice before it is acted on. SP is expected to accept the single directive for gear and flaps and configure with the Leader.

error_modes.label: Cross-check of the Leader's configuration and thumbs up exchange

texts.0: SP, due to returning the thumbs up as a reflex without actually checking Number 1's gear and flaps, passed a configuration that had not been verified before the gear down call was transmitted. The long unfocused look also took the sight picture out of the scan and the aircraft climbed and went wide beyond the outer allowance, more than 10 ft above the Leader's wing line, requiring IP intervention. The purpose of the cross-check was not applied.
texts.1: SP, due to breaking the wing reference for an extended stare at the Leader's landing gear rather than a deliberate glance, let the position drift out to the outer tolerance during the check, reaching the 10 ft limit above the wing line with about 30 ft of lateral separation. The thumbs up was given only after the IP prompted and the position was recovered on the same call. The tolerances were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check taken in one long look instead of split between the gear, the flaps and the sight picture, allowed the position to open past the tighter band to roughly 25 ft of lateral separation while remaining inside the outer allowance. The Leader's configuration was correctly verified and the thumbs up given, and SP re-established the position without being told.
texts.3: SP checked Number 1's gear and flap configuration and gave the thumbs up, then confirmed the Leader's return signal before the gear down call. The check was taken in short glances that kept the sight picture in the scan and the position stayed inside 20 ft of lateral separation and within a few feet of the wing line.
texts.4: SP verified the Leader's configuration item by item and passed the thumbs up with no interruption to the wing reference. Lateral separation held on the 10 ft reference point and the vertical position did not move off the wing line during the exchange. The signal was returned and acknowledged before the gear down call without any delay.
texts.marginal: SP completed the cross-check and the thumbs up exchange within standards, but the signal was given before the flaps had been looked at and the position loosened toward the edge of the tighter band while the check was made. The trend is toward a signal passed to complete the sequence rather than to confirm the Leader's configuration. SP is expected to verify both gear and flaps in short glances that keep the sight picture in the scan.

error_modes.label: Flap setting other than TO for the formation approach

texts.0: SP, due to reverting to the single ship habit of selecting LDG flaps, configured with more drag than the Leader on an approach that is flown with flaps in the TO position. The aircraft decelerated and sank aft and low, going beyond 30 ft of lateral separation and more than 5 ft below the Leader's wing line, and the IP intervened to reset the flaps to TO and recover the position. The configuration difference was not recognized as the cause.
texts.1: SP, due to selecting LDG flaps before checking the briefed formation approach configuration, carried extra drag until the error was called. The deceleration took the position out to the outer allowance, about 30 ft of lateral separation with the observance angle at the 55 degree edge, and the flaps were returned to TO only after the IP directed it. The tolerances were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to moving the flap handle past the TO position before catching it, briefly carried more drag than the Leader and fell aft past the tighter band to roughly 25 ft of lateral separation, still inside the outer allowance. SP identified the wrong setting immediately, reset the flaps to TO and closed the position back down with a coordinated power input.
texts.3: SP set the flaps to the TO position for the formation approach and matched the Leader's drag and deceleration. The position held within the tighter fingertip band, lateral separation inside 20 ft and vertical position within a few feet of the wing line, through the configuration change and down the approach.
texts.4: SP selected TO flaps without hesitation and led the drag change with power so the sight picture did not move. Lateral separation stayed on the 10 ft reference point and the observance angle held 30 degrees through the approach. The configuration matched the Leader exactly for the whole descent.
texts.marginal: SP flew the approach with flaps in the TO position and within standards, but the handle was checked against the LDG detent before the correct selection was made and the resulting hesitation let the position sag to the edge of the tighter band. The trend is toward carrying single ship configuration habits into the formation approach. SP is expected to set TO flaps directly and anticipate the smaller drag change.

error_modes.label: Side positioning for the penetration turn and the upwind side of the runway

texts.0: SP, due to not moving to the side opposite the direction of the penetration turn when Number 1 set the formation up for the approach, was left on the inside of the turn and on the downwind side of the landing runway. When the turn was started the position could not be held from the inside, separation closed inside the 10 ft reference point and the observance angle went beyond 55 degrees, and the IP took control to reposition the aircraft. The requirement to be on the upwind side was not recognized.
texts.1: SP, due to starting the reposition to the correct side only after the penetration turn had begun, crossed under late and arrived on the outer allowance, about 30 ft of lateral separation with the observance angle at the 55 degree edge. The correct side was taken up only after the IP directed the move and the position was rebuilt from there. The tolerances were not exceeded.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow reading of the Leader's setup for the approach, was late recognizing the need to be on the side opposite the penetration turn and repositioned with a compressed cross under that opened the position past the tighter band to roughly 25 ft of lateral separation, still inside the outer allowance. SP settled the crossing rate early and re-established the correct side unassisted.
texts.3: SP took up the side opposite the direction of the penetration turn and on the upwind side of the landing runway before the approach was started. The reposition was flown with a controlled crossing rate and the position stayed within the tighter fingertip band, lateral separation inside 20 ft and the observance angle within 30 plus or minus 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP anticipated the direction of the penetration turn from the Leader's setup and was already established on the correct upwind side before the approach began. The reposition produced no excursion, with lateral separation on the 10 ft reference point and the vertical position steady on the wing line. No further adjustment was needed through the turn.
texts.marginal: SP was on the correct side for the penetration turn within standards, but the move was made only after the Leader's intentions became obvious and the crossing rate had to be checked at the end. The trend is toward reacting to the turn rather than positioning for it. SP is expected to work out the direction of the penetration turn in advance and take the upwind side before the approach starts.
